AIML Module Project - Neural Networks - Aaditya Kumar Ravi¶

• DOMAIN: Electronics and Telecommunication
• CONTEXT: A communications equipment manufacturing company has a product which is responsible for emitting informative signals. Company wants to build a machine learning model which can help the company to predict the equipment’s signal quality using various parameters.
• DATA DESCRIPTION: The data set contains information on various signal tests performed:

  1. Parameters: Various measurable signal parameters.
  2. Signal_Quality: Final signal strength or quality

• PROJECT OBJECTIVE: To build a classifier which can use the given parameters to determine the signal strength or quality.
Steps and tasks: [ Total Score: 30 Marks]

E. Share insights from the initial data analysis (at least 2). [2 Marks]¶

Insights:

  • Signal Strength varies from 3 to 8.
  • Majority of the equipments have signal strength of 5 followed by signal strength of 6 and then 7.
  • There are only 10 devices which has minimum signal strength of 3.
  • There are 17 devices having very high signal strength i.e 8
  • There are 53 devices with signal strength of 4.

3. Model Training & Evaluation using Neural Network [13 Marks]¶

A. Design a Neural Network to train a classifier. [3 Marks]¶

AND¶

B. Train the classifier using previously designed Architecture [2 Marks]¶

In [97]:
model = Sequential() #initialize neural network

model.add(Dense(64, input_shape=(11,), activation='relu')) #input layer with 64 neurons, 11 features and relu activation function
model.add(Dense(32, activation='relu')) #hidden layer with 32 neurons and relu activation function
#since target variable Signal_Strength column has 6 classes, we will have 6 neurons in the output layer and will use softmax activation function as it 
#is multiclass classification problem
model.add(Dense(6, activation='softmax'))
In [98]:
model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy']) #compile the model
In [99]:
model.summary()

In [104]:
model_1 = Sequential([
    Dense(64, input_shape=(11,), activation='relu'),
    Dropout(0.2),
    Dense(32, activation='relu'),
    Dropout(0.2),
    Dense(6, activation='softmax')
])

optimizer = optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.001)
model_1.compile(optimizer=optimizer, loss='categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])

history_1 = model_1.fit(X_train, Y_train, epochs=100, batch_size=16, validation_split=0.2) #training the model with increased number of epochs and smaller batch size

Model 2: Adding batch normalization to the previous model, let us see the performance

In [106]:
model_2 = Sequential([
    Dense(64, input_shape=(11,), activation='relu'),
    BatchNormalization(), 
    Dropout(0.2),
    Dense(32, activation='relu'),
    BatchNormalization(), 
    Dropout(0.2),
    Dense(6, activation='softmax')
])

optimizer = optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.001)
model_2.compile(optimizer=optimizer, loss='categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])

history_2 = model_2.fit(X_train, Y_train, epochs=100, batch_size=16, validation_split=0.2)

Insights:

  • Training loss is higher than validation loss upto around 40 epochs, which suggests that the model is overfitting training data.

  • but after 40 epochs, training loss is sometime lower or qual to validation loss, which has improved performance a bit.

  • At 100 epochs training loss is lesser than validation loss, which is good.

  • Training accuracy is lower than validation accuracy which is an unusual condition, there might be something wrong, may be due to target class imbalancing issue or something else. but overall so far achieved accuracy score is 58.5% on training data, 62.8% on validation data and 53% on testing data.

  • However in previous case, we got just an accuracy of 50% on training data, 49% on validation data and 50% on testing data.

  • If we see loss in current model, loss is minimized. Current model training loss is 0.98, validation loss is 0.96, whereas loss in previous model was higher than this, it was 1.12 on training and 1.09 on validation.

Part B - 30 Marks¶

• DOMAIN: Autonomous Vehicles
• CONTEXT: A Recognising multi-digit numbers in photographs captured at street level is an important component of modern-day map making. A classic example of a corpus of such street-level photographs is Google’s Street View imagery composed of hundreds of millions of geo-located 360-degree panoramic images.

The ability to automatically transcribe an address number from a geo-located patch of pixels and associate the transcribed number with a known street address helps pinpoint, with a high degree of accuracy, the location of the building it represents. More broadly, recognising numbers in photographs is a problem of interest to the optical character recognition community.

While OCR on constrained domains like document processing is well studied, arbitrary multi-character text recognition in photographs is still highly challenging. This difficulty arises due to the wide variability in the visual appearance of text in the wild on account of a large range of fonts, colours, styles, orientations, and character arrangements.

The recognition problem is further complicated by environmental factors such as lighting, shadows, specularity, and occlusions as well as by image acquisition factors such as resolution, motion, and focus blurs. In this project, we will use the dataset with images centred around a single digit (many of the images do contain some distractors at the sides). Although we are taking a sample of the data which is simpler, it is more complex than MNIST because of the distractors.

• DATA DESCRIPTION: The SVHN is a real-world image dataset for developing machine learning and object recognition algorithms with the minimal requirement on data formatting but comes from a significantly harder, unsolved, real-world problem (recognising digits and numbers in natural scene images). SVHN is obtained from house numbers in Google Street View images.

Where the labels for each of this image are the prominent number in that image i.e. 2,6,7 and 4 respectively.
The dataset has been provided in the form of h5py files. You can read about this file format here: https://docs.h5py.org/en/stable/ Acknowledgement: Yuval Netzer, Tao Wang, Adam Coates, Alessandro Bissacco, Bo Wu, Andrew Y. Ng Reading Digits in Natural Images with Unsupervised Feature Learning NIPS Workshop on Deep Learning and Unsupervised Feature Learning 2011. PDF http://ufldl.stanford.edu/housenumbers as the URL for this site.

• PROJECT OBJECTIVE: To build a digit classifier on the SVHN (Street View Housing Number) dataset.

Model with very slow learning rate 0.0001 and 10 epochs

  • We have used batch normalization, dropout reglurarization techniques and tried different number of hidden layers to make improved model. Also evaluated model with different number of hidden layers and unit counts in that and designed the neural network as below:
In [125]:
image_size=32*32

model = Sequential()  

model.add(Dense(512, activation='relu',kernel_initializer='he_uniform',input_shape=(image_size,)))
model.add(BatchNormalization()) 
model.add(Dense(256, activation='relu',kernel_initializer='he_uniform'))
model.add(Dense(256, activation='relu',kernel_initializer='he_uniform'))
model.add(Dropout(0.5))
model.add(Dense(128, activation='relu',kernel_initializer='he_uniform'))
model.add(Dense(128, activation='relu',kernel_initializer='he_uniform'))
model.add(Dropout(0.5))
model.add(Dense(64, activation='relu',kernel_initializer='he_uniform'))
model.add(Dense(64, activation='relu',kernel_initializer='he_uniform'))

model.add(Dense(num_classes_count, activation='softmax'))

adam = optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.0001)
model.compile(loss=tf.losses.categorical_crossentropy, optimizer=adam, metrics=['accuracy'])

model.summary()

checkpoint = ModelCheckpoint("model_weights.weights.h5",monitor='val_accuracy',
                          save_weights_only=True, mode='max',verbose=1)
reduce_learningrate = ReduceLROnPlateau(monitor='val_loss',factor=0.1,patience=2,min_lr=0.00001,model='auto')
callbacks = [checkpoint,reduce_learningrate]

history=model.fit(X_train, Y_train, validation_data=(X_val, Y_val), epochs=10, batch_size=512, verbose=2,callbacks=callbacks)

image_size=32*32

model = Sequential()  

model.add(Dense(512, activation='relu',kernel_initializer='he_uniform',input_shape=(image_size,)))
model.add(BatchNormalization()) 
model.add(Dense(256, activation='relu',kernel_initializer='he_uniform'))
model.add(Dense(256, activation='relu',kernel_initializer='he_uniform'))
model.add(Dropout(0.5))
model.add(Dense(128, activation='relu',kernel_initializer='he_uniform'))
model.add(Dense(128, activation='relu',kernel_initializer='he_uniform'))
model.add(Dropout(0.5))
model.add(Dense(64, activation='relu',kernel_initializer='he_uniform'))
model.add(Dense(64, activation='relu',kernel_initializer='he_uniform'))

model.add(Dense(num_classes_count, activation='softmax'))

adam = optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.001)
model.compile(loss=tf.losses.categorical_crossentropy, optimizer=adam, metrics=['accuracy'])

model.summary()

checkpoint = ModelCheckpoint("model_weights.weights.h5",monitor='val_accuracy',
                          save_weights_only=True, mode='max',verbose=1)
reduce_learningrate = ReduceLROnPlateau(monitor='val_loss',factor=0.1,patience=2,min_lr=0.00001,model='auto')
callbacks = [checkpoint,reduce_learningrate]

history=model.fit(X_train, Y_train, validation_data=(X_val, Y_val), epochs=50, batch_size=512, verbose=2,callbacks=callbacks)

print('=============Classification Report==========')
print(classification_report(preserved_actual_Y_test,Y_pred_final))

cm=confusion_matrix(preserved_actual_Y_test,Y_pred_final)
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.imshow(cm, cmap='Blues', interpolation='nearest')
plt.colorbar()
plt.xlabel('Predicted')
plt.ylabel('Actual')
for i in range(len(cm)):
    for j in range(len(cm[i])):
        plt.text(j, i, str(cm[i][j]), ha='center', va='center', color='black')
plt.show()

print("==========Misclassfied images===============")
index = 0
misclassified_images = []
for label, predict in zip(preserved_actual_Y_test, Y_pred_final):
    if label != predict: 
        misclassified_images.append(index)
    index +=1
print("List of misclassified images:",misclassified_images)
print("Total count of misclassified images",len(misclassified_images))

  • On training data, we have loss of 0.53 and accuracy of 83%.
  • On validation data, we have loss of 0.57 and accuracy of almost 82%
  • On test data, we have loss of 0.66 and accuracy of almost 80%
  • We have seen quite good result of improvement on the model.
  • If we look at classification report, it has a good balanced overall classwise accuracy, recall, precision, f1 score of 80 to 85% for all the classes, which is good.
  • Though there are 3543 misclassified images.
  • Let us keep this as final model for now. but this is true that this model also has scope of improvement.

D. Plot the training loss, validation loss vs number of epochs and training accuracy, validation accuracy vs number of epochs plot and write your observations on the same. [4 Marks]¶

In [131]:
h = pd.DataFrame(history.history)
h['epoch'] = history.epoch
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.ylabel('Loss')
plt.title("Training Loss, Validation Loss vs Epochs")
plt.plot(h['loss'])
plt.plot(h['val_loss'])
plt.legend(("training" , "validation") , loc=0);
In [132]:
plt.title("Training Accuracy, Validation Accuracy vs Epochs")
plt.plot(h['accuracy'])
plt.plot(h['val_accuracy'])
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.ylabel('Accuracy')
plt.legend(("Training" , "Validation") , loc=0);

Insights:

  • Training loss starts higher and decreases rapidly than validation loss upto around 15 epochs which means model is learning data quite well.
  • Training loss start from 2.25 and falls at 0.75 rapidly.
  • Training and validation both losses are going together, we don't see much fluctuations which is good.
  • Training and validation both accuracy is going up together with epochs, we don't see much fluctuations which is good.
  • Accuracy of 83% on training, 82% on validation is good and tells that it is a good model as score on test data is also 80% which is nearby training scores which tells it is not an overfit moel but yet there is scope of improvement on model accuracy.
